lesson.title: What the Next Sale Is Worth: Marginal Revenue
lesson.summary: Marginal revenue, R'(x), is the derivative of total revenue and estimates the extra income from selling one more unit; it often falls as quantity rises because selling more usually means charging less per unit.
lesson.body:
Total revenue is price times quantity, R(x) = p(x) * x, where p(x) is the price per unit when x units are sold. In most markets, p(x) is a decreasing function of x, a demand curve: selling more units generally requires charging a lower price to attract enough buyers. Marginal revenue, MR(x) = R'(x), estimates the extra income earned from selling exactly one more unit at the current sales level.

It is tempting to assume marginal revenue just equals the current price, since that is what the next buyer pays. But when price depends on quantity, selling one more unit typically means every unit, not just the new one, sells at a slightly lower price than it otherwise would have. That effect pulls marginal revenue below the current price for any demand curve that slopes downward, a pattern the worked example below shows directly.

Suppose demand for a product follows p(x) = 100 - 0.5x dollars per unit. Total revenue is R(x) = x * p(x) = 100x - 0.5x^2, so R'(x) = 100 - x. At x = 30 units sold, MR(30) = 100 - 30 = 70 dollars, meaning the 31st sale is predicted to add about $70 to total revenue. Checking directly: R(30) = 100(30) - 0.5(900) = 2550 dollars, and R(31) = 100(31) - 0.5(961) = 2619.5 dollars, an actual gain of 2619.5 - 2550 = 69.5 dollars, matching the $70 estimate to within fifty cents. Meanwhile the price at x = 30 is p(30) = 100 - 0.5(30) = 85 dollars, noticeably higher than the $70 marginal revenue, exactly the gap created by needing to lower the price on all units to sell one more.

Tracking marginal revenue tells a business whether selling more is still paying off, a question that only becomes fully answered once marginal revenue is compared against marginal cost, the subject of the next chapter.
